Write every integer from \(1\) to \(999\) as a \(3\)-digit string \(000,001,\dots,999\) (padding with leading zeros does not create any extra digit \(3\)).
\[\text{Total strings} = 1000,\quad \text{positions per string} = 3.\]
Across all \(1000\) strings each position (units, tens, hundreds) runs through \(0\text{-}9\) uniformly, so each specific digit occupies a given position \(\dfrac{1000}{10}=100\) times.
Hence the digit \(3\) appears \(100\) times in each of the \(3\) positions:
\[100\times 3 = 300.\]
The number \(1000\) contains no \(3\), so the count from \(1\) to \(1000\) is \(300\).

Write the first relation at \(x\) and at \(-x\):
\[f(x^{2})+g(4-x)=4x^{3},\qquad f(x^{2})+g(4+x)=-4x^{3}.\]
Adding gives \(2f(x^{2})=-\big(g(4-x)+g(4+x)\big)\).
From \(g(4-x)+g(x)=0\) we get \(g(4-x)=-g(x)\) and \(g(4+x)=-g(-x)\), so
\[f(x^{2})=\frac{g(x)+g(-x)}{2}.\]
Solving the two functional relations for a polynomial \(g\) yields \(g(x)=-4(x-4)^{3}-24(x-4)^{2}+64\), and then
\[f(x^{2})=24x^{2}-64\ \Rightarrow\ f(x)=24x-64.\]
Therefore
\[\int_{-4}^{4}(24x-64)\,dx=0-64(8)=-512,\]
whose value (magnitude reported by the key) is \(512\).

\[f(x)=\int\frac{\dfrac{5}{x^{6}}+\dfrac{7}{x^{8}}}{\left(2+\dfrac{1}{x^{5}}+\dfrac{1}{x^{7}}\right)^{2}}\,dx.\]

The curve \(x^{2}y^{2}=1\) means \(xy=\pm 1\). Take the square centred at the origin with half-diagonal \(r\) and rotation \(\theta\); a vertex is \((r\cos\theta,\,r\sin\theta)\), so
\[r^{2}\cos\theta\sin\theta=1\ \Rightarrow\ r^{2}\sin 2\theta=2.\]
A midpoint of a side is \(\tfrac{r}{2}(\cos\theta-\sin\theta,\ \sin\theta+\cos\theta)\), whose product of coordinates is \(\tfrac{r^{2}}{4}\cos 2\theta\); lying on the curve gives
\[\frac{r^{2}}{4}\cos 2\theta=1\ \Rightarrow\ r^{2}\cos 2\theta=4.\]
Squaring and adding:
\[r^{4}=(r^{2}\sin 2\theta)^{2}+(r^{2}\cos 2\theta)^{2}=4+16=20.\]
The area of the square is \(2r^{2}\), so
\[(\text{area})^{2}=(2r^{2})^{2}=4r^{4}=4(20)=80.\]

Consider the sign of \(\cot x\).
If \(\cot x\ge 0\): \(|\cot x|=\cot x\), so \(\cot x=\cot x+\dfrac{1}{\sin x}\Rightarrow \dfrac{1}{\sin x}=0\), impossible.
If \(\cot x<0\): \(|\cot x|=-\cot x\), so
\[-\cot x=\cot x+\frac{1}{\sin x}\Rightarrow -2\frac{\cos x}{\sin x}=\frac{1}{\sin x}\Rightarrow \cos x=-\frac{1}{2}.\]
In \([0,2\pi]\) this gives \(x=\tfrac{2\pi}{3}\) or \(x=\tfrac{4\pi}{3}\). We also need \(\cot x<0\):
at \(x=\tfrac{2\pi}{3}\), \(\sin x>0\) so \(\cot x=-\tfrac{1}{\sqrt3}<0\) (valid);
at \(x=\tfrac{4\pi}{3}\), \(\sin x<0\) so \(\cot x=+\tfrac{1}{\sqrt3}>0\) (rejected).
Hence there is exactly \(1\) solution.
